entries.title: How Jeffery Simmons immediately became the face — and voice — of the Bears defense
entries.summary: <p>It didn’t take Jeffery Simmons long to become the face of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> defense.</p><p>And the mouth. And the legs.</p><p>On Sunday night, Simmons identified a screen from his spot at defensive tackle and hustled toward the right flat. When Emeka Egbuka caught the screen pass, Simmons changed his angle upfield. Twenty-one yards later, at full sprint, he dove and tripped up the Buccaneers receiver.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">This <a href="https://x.com/GrindSimmons94?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@GrindSimmons94</a> chase-down angle is absolutely terrifying 😳<a href="https://x.com/ChicagoBears?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@ChicagoBears</a> | <a href="https://x.com/insidetheNFL?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@InsideTheNFL</a> <a href="https://t.co/4gGEMNyep7">pic.twitter.com/4gGEMNyep7</a></p>— NFL Films (@NFLFilms) <a href="https://x.com/NFLFilms/status/2119905749866356742?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 9, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Defensive end Daniel Hardy, who was the closest defensive lineman to the play — until Simmons went racing past him — couldn’t believe it.</p><p>“It motivates everybody,” he said. “When the biggest person on the field is running harder and faster than anybody else, you don’t have an excuse anymore.”</p><p>When coaches and executives use the word, it’s easy to roll your eyes. But in Simmons’ case, it’s true — he’s been a multiplier. He’s made his teammates better by drawing double teams and giving them one fewer man to beat, but also by playing so hard that they can’t help but do the same.</p><p>“When offenses know they can’t run the ball inside, they try to get the ball to the perimeter on screens, on tosses. …” Simmons said. “That’s just my game. That’s what I take a lot of pride in, just being around the ball … He had the ball in his hand, and that’s the most important thing on the field.”</p><p>When the Bears <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/29/bears-titans-trade-jeffery-simmons-first-round-picks-massive-swing-nfl" >traded two first-round picks and a fourth-rounder to the Titans for Simmons</a>, it was clear that he’d have to play to a remarkable standard to be worth the investment.</p><p>He’s done all that, and more, thus far.</p><p>Watching Simmons <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/03/new-dt-jeffery-simmons-bears-debut-was-everything-both-sides-dreamed-of-in-34-17-win-over-seahawks" >dominate the Seahawks on “Monday Night Football,”</a> one Bears front office executive said out loud, to no one in particular, that he was expensive — but worth it. </p><p>On a franchise known for their defensive stars — from Brian Urlacher to Dan Hampton, Mike Singletary to Richard Dent — Simmons fit in from the second he arrived. He hasn’t needed an adjustment period. He played 87% of the Bears’ snaps against the Seahawks and 97% against the Buccaneers. His 121 snaps are the second-most by any defensive tackle over those two weeks.</p><p>“I’ll use this week very wisely,” he said of the bye, “to take care of my body.”</p><p>The outside world has taken note of his play. Simmons — and even his 3-year-old daughter Mulani — has been the centerpiece of two straight primetime games. Inside Halas Hall, teammates and coaches who have known him for mere days speak with a reverent tone not heard since Khalil Mack played defensive end.</p><p>“His football character bleeds off the tape,” defensive coordinator Dennis Allen said. “It bled off the tape in Tennessee. It bled off the tape … in Seattle. He plays the game tough. He plays the game violently. He plays the game hard …</p><p>“Why does he raise the level of other guys around him? Because when your best players work the way that he works, the way that he practices, prepares the way that he prepares, and then plays the game the way that he plays, you don't have a choice but to raise your level.”</p><p>Former Steelers coach Mike Tomlin, who was in town to cover the Bears-Buccaneers, noticed.</p><p>“I don’t even attempt to hide my man crush for this guy,” he said on NBC. “He’s top of the food chain in the D-tackle position … he’s got it all. He checks all of the boxes. He’s a power player that happens to be athletic. He’s smart, he’s got natural leadership skills, and I love his surly disposition, which is an asset.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Mike Tomlin’s monologue on Jeffery Simmons is immaculate 😂 <a href="https://t.co/VEVFlRKDtK">pic.twitter.com/VEVFlRKDtK</a></p>— Coach Dan Casey (@CoachDanCasey) <a href="https://x.com/CoachDanCasey/status/2119595497803612608?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 9, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>The Buccaneers didn’t think so. After the Bears beat them, tackle Luke Goedeke said Simmons grabbed his jersey so the Bears’ defensive ends could run free. Quarterback Baker Mayfield <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/09/bears-buccaneers-qb-baker-mayfield-accuse-mimicking-snap-count-cadence" >also said the Bears’ defensive linemen were barking out snap counts</a> and got his linemen to commit false starts.</p><p>Grousing about Simmons around the league continued Monday, when the Jaguars traded a 2027 first-round draft pick and a 2029 second-rounder to the Eagles for a lesser defensive tackle, Jordan Davis. The Bears’ trade, by comparison, looks far more reasonable — even if the cost might someday sting. </p><p>Simmons’ Pro Football Focus pass rush grade ranks third among defensive tackles who have played at least half their team’s snaps the past two weeks. With Simmons on their roster, Allen has blitzed just 23% of the time, compared to 42% of the time in Weeks 1-7 — and has been more successful getting to the quarterback.</p><p>In the second half Sunday night, the Bears got pressure on Mayfield 41% of the time despite blitzing just twice on 17 passes. When the Bears needed it most, Simmons provided one of the Bears’ four second-half sacks.</p><p>“Credit to Jeff,” Hardy said. “This is his second game with the team and he’s been a leader already, just telling guys that, 'We need to keep going, we need to keep hunting, don’t be scared.' …</p><p>“We have some hungry, foaming-at-the-mouth dogs in the D-line room, and they want to get after the QB.”</p><p>That includes Montez Sweat, his former Mississippi State teammate. Since the Bears traded for Simmons, both Sweat and edge rusher Austin Booker rank in the top 28 in PFF’s pass rush scores.</p><p>Sweat credited the jolt the Bears got from his old friend.</p><p>“He’s always had a real love for the game,” Sweat said, “and that’s infectious across the whole line, and whole team.”</p>

entries.title: State Rep. Kam Buckner says he's the right person to succeed Chris Welch as House speaker
entries.summary: <p>State Rep. Kam Buckner (D-Chicago) on Wednesday made his case to replace his ally Emanuel "Chris" Welch as Illinois House speaker, arguing that it doesn't have to take a woman to clean up Springfield’s entrenched culture of sexual harassment.</p><p>Buckner is a trusted Welch lieutenant who has served the now-outgoing speaker as assistant majority leader and speaker pro tempore.</p><p>He was part of the working group Welch created last summer in response to explosive revelations that Welch was aware of sexual harassment allegations against disgraced ex-State Rep. Harry Benton (D-Plainfield) almost three years before additional complaints prompted Benton’s resignation. </p><p>Buckner has also served as the speaker’s point man on high-profile House issues ranging from the Bears stadium saga to the state budget — and the $1.5 million mass transit bailout that replaced the Regional Transit Authority with the newly created Northern Illinois Transit Authority.</p><p>Buckner is now making a strong play for the job of House speaker, after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/11/05/illinois-house-speaker-chris-welch-mutiny-26-democrats-call-for-new-leader-harry-benton-scandal" >26 House Democrats publicly demanded</a> Welch's ouster from the post. Welch decided to not seek another term as speaker. </p><p>“I’ve served in multiple leadership roles and I’ve worked on some of the most complex issues that have faced this state — from transit to budget to stadiums,” Buckner told the Sun-Times. “I’ve spent much of my own career building consensus among people who don’t necessarily agree with each other out of the gate.”</p><p>Welch’s exit was a repeat of past history.</p><p> Mishandling of sexual harassment allegations also marked the beginning of the end for Welch’s predecessor and mentor — now-convicted Illinois House Speaker Michael Madigan.</p><p>The back-to-back sexual harassment scandals in the speaker’s office could pave the way for a woman to become Illinois <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/11/06/illinois-house-speaker-chris-welch-steps-down-female-replacement-contenders" >first female House speaker. </a>Five women currently serving in the House have been among those mentioned as possible successors.</p><p>Buckner said the election of a woman would be “historically significant” and “not symbolic at all” because there are so many “accomplished women in our caucus who have worked on huge pieces of legislation.”</p><p>But he argued that the next speaker doesn’t necessarily need to be a woman to finally rid the chamber of the longstanding bias against women. The Benton scandal raised questions about Welch’s own behavior — his social media interactions with a complainant in the case left the young woman uncomfortable, for which he later apologized.</p><p> </p><p>“It’s not gonna be the person with the gavel that’s fixing the culture. It’s the person with the gavel that’s giving the representatives the ability to fix their own house, to fix their culture, give them the resources and tools they need. Not creating a system where there’s gonna be retaliation if you say something they don’t like,” Buckner said.</p><p>“I don’t think it’s as binary as just saying it has to be a person in this space who is of a certain demographic… If we keep focusing on personalities, well be back in the same position in six years.”</p><p>If elected speaker, Buckner said he would work to implement a strict code of conduct that makes it “very clear what we will and what we won’t accept.” He would also change Welch’s much-criticized internal mandate that legislation garner support from 60 House Democrats to qualify for being called for a vote on the House floor.</p><p>"The 60-vote rule was created in order to foster and engender some unity withing our caucus. In some instances, it actually had the opposite effect," Buckner said. "I don't feel like the way forward is to continue... the 60-vote rule... But that would require stronger processes through the committee process to make certain that bills that may be detrimental to the state and to our caucus unity go through a more rigorous conversation."</p><p>A former football standout at the University of Illinois, Buckner was not about to give his competitors for the speaker’s gavel any bulletin board material to be used against him.</p><p>Buckner said he does not believe the leadership vacuum created by Welch’s impending exit will make it difficult for lawmakers to finally resolve the Bears’ stadium saga.</p><p>Months of intense<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/06/bears-stadium-roger-goodell-nfl-commissioner-george-mccaskey-kevin-warren-chicago-arlington-heights-meeting-hammond-indiana" > negotiations</a> with NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell, Gov. JB Pritzker and Bears ownership have centered on a stadium authority model that gives Chicago lawmakers political cover to support, because it cracks the door open to a salad bar of Chicago sites that the Bears appear to have considered and dismissed.</p><p>“The Bears only own one piece of land in the United States of America — and that is the former Arlington Park” racecourse site, Buckner said. “Business acumen would tell you if you spend a couple hundred million dollars on a piece of land, you wan to try and find a way to make it work.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-d80000" name="html-embed-module-d80000"></a><iframe allow="monetization" frameborder="0" height="200" scrolling="no" src="https://play.prx.org/e?ge=prx_12963_3cc5fd35-3e02-4d1d-8d10-82ec824e2de2&uf=https%3A%2F%2Fpublicfeeds.net%2Ff%2F12963%2Ffeed-rss.xml " style="min-width: 300px;" width="100%"></iframe> </div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Bears QB Caleb Williams celebrates platinum glove with Pete Crow-Armstrong
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> quarterback Caleb Williams joined Pete Crow-Armstrong this week to celebrate the Cubs star winning the Platinum Glove for his work in center field.</p><p>Crow-Armstrong, of course, has a bigger award at stake this week — the National League MVP award will be handed out Thursday.</p><p>Williams, Crow-Armstrong and Cole Bennett — aka “Lyrical Lemonade” — were among those who celebrated Monday at Adalina Prime, which printed out a customized, albeit AI-centric, menu congratulating the Cubs star. The steakhouse is located in Fulton Market.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Caleb Williams supporting Pete Crow-Armstrong’s Gold/Platinum Glove 🏆 <a href="https://t.co/mzsidq91hW">pic.twitter.com/mzsidq91hW</a></p>— Cubs Zone (@CubsZone) <a href="https://x.com/CubsZone/status/2120016480196579797?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 10, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Williams posted a photo of Crow-Armstrong posing with the menu on social media, calling him a “legend.”</p><p>After meeting Monday to go over film from their win against the Buccaneers, Bears coach Ben Johnson gave his team the rest of the week off. The Collective Bargaining Agreement states that NFL teams must be off from Thursday-Sunday during their bye week.</p><p>The last Cubs player voted NL MVP was Kris Bryant in 2016.</p>

entries.title: 2 lawsuits allege Salvation Army youth pastor sexually abused three children in Chicago suburbs
entries.summary: <p>Three women came forward Wednesday to say they've carried the lasting effects of sexual abuse they endured as children at the hands of a Salvation Army youth pastor for nearly three decades — along with the burden of what they describe as the institution’s failure to protect them.</p><p>Attorneys for Kristy Wynveen, Lindsey Gauthier and Anna Kozak announced two lawsuits filed Tuesday in Cook County Circuit Court against the Salvation Army, alleging its leaders knew about the abuse at a west suburban community center in the 1990s but allowed it to continue for years.</p><p>The three spoke publicly for the first time about their experiences, saying they hope to hold the national faith-based organization accountable and encourage other survivors to come forward.</p><p>“The effect that this has had on me has reached every dark corner of my life, every relationship that I've ever had. Every thought, every action is tainted with the abuse that happened,” Kozak said. “That's a struggle that I have to carry, that Lindsey and Kristy have to carry, and that many other survivors of sexual abuse have to carry.”</p><p>Wynveen, Gauthier and Kozak said they were sexually abused by a youth pastor named Brian Davis between 1996 and 2002 at the Salvation Army’s Tri-City Corps Community Center in St. Charles. The women were as young as 11, according to the lawsuits.</p><p>Kozak is expected to file a separate complaint, said Mike Grieco, lead attorney representing the women.</p><p>The complaints describe a pattern of grooming and sexual abuse and allege that Salvation Army leaders, including a social services director and an officer, knew about Davis’ inappropriate conduct but failed to intervene.</p><p>The lawsuits name the Salvation Army’s USA Central Territory, Tri-City Corps and National Corporation as defendants, alleging negligence and other failures that allowed the abuse to take place under the organization’s watch.</p><p>“It fires me up as a litigator to make sure that we get a pound of flesh in these cases,” Grieco said. “That the wrong people can get a spotlight shown on them, so that people can get justice after decades of suffering.”</p><p>The Chicago-based firm specializes in sexual abuse litigation against faith-based institutions, including the Archdiocese of Chicago, Grieco said. He said allegations of abuse within the organization extend beyond its Illinois operations.</p><p>“There is a systemic issue related to abuse against the Salvation Army,” he said. “There's lots of cases around the country that we've seen based on public dockets, and it's something that I think is coming to light more and more now.”</p><p>The lawsuits follow other sexual abuse cases connected to the Salvation Army in Chicago. In 2016, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2016/12/29/18364564/suit-kroc-center-negligent-in-sexual-assault-at-pool " target="_blank" >the organization was sued for negligence </a>over allegations that two minors were sexually abused at the Kroc Center in West Pullman. And in 2024, John Kim, a youth pastor at the Salvation Army Mayfair Community Church on Chicago’s Northwest Side, <a class="Link" href="https://www.cbsnews.com/chicago/news/chicago-pastor-sexual-abuse-victims/" target="_blank" >pleaded guilty to aggravated battery</a> in a case involving the sexual abuse of a minor, CBS Chicago reported.</p><p>Brian Duewel, a spokesperson for the Salvation Army’s North and Central Illinois Division, said in an email to the Sun-Times that the organization considers the safety and well-being of participants in its programs paramount and that any allegation of sexual misconduct is “deeply concerning.”</p><p>Duewel said the Salvation Army learned in early 2025 of four complaints against Davis dating back to the 1990s involving sexual misconduct with teenage girls. He said the organization had spent more than a year working to understand the allegations and engage with the claimants and their attorneys</p><p>All claims had gone through mediation and one had been resolved, Duewel said. The organization encourages anyone who may have been harmed by Davis to contact authorities.</p><p>"Mr. Davis has not been affiliated with The Salvation Army for more than two decades, and he will never again be employed by or serve with the Salvation Army in any capacity," Duewel said.</p><p>Grieco clarified that none of the three women’s cases had been resolved, and said it remains unclear how long Davis continued working in ministry with the Salvation Army. </p><p>Davis pleaded guilty in 2003 to criminal sexual abuse involving Wynveen in Kane County Circuit Court, according to court documents. He was sentenced to 36 months probation and 60 days of periodic imprisonment, and was registered as a sex offender.</p><p>The complaints allege that the Salvation Army never conducted its own investigation, even after Davis faced criminal prosecution. The attorneys hope the litigation will establish what the organization knew about his conduct, when it learned of the allegations and what steps, if any, it took in response.</p><p>“[The Salvation Army] knows something, and we need to discover what all of that is,” Grieco said.</p><p>The attorneys are also seeking information from former Salvation Army employees, volunteers, officers, youth group members and parents who may have witnessed or heard about Davis’ conduct.</p><p>For the women, speaking publicly is also a way to challenge the silence they say has compounded the harm of the abuse.</p><p>“The culture of the world that we live in right now is to sweep things under the rug, and to blame the victims, and to take the easiest out possible,” Kozak said. “We need to change that. And that is why I'm standing here right now talking about what happened to me.”</p>

entries.title: 'Totalmente evitable’: hombre del área de Chicago muere tras vuelo de deportación
entries.summary: <p>Un hombre del área de Chicago que no tenía antecedentes penales y padecía múltiples afecciones crónicas murió poco después de un vuelo de deportación a Pakistán, dijo su abogado el martes.</p><p>Ayaz Ahmed, de 61 años y residente de Morton Grove, fue arrestado en junio por la Oficina de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas (ICE) y enfrentaba la deportación por tener una visa vencida, dijo su abogado Hashim Siddique. Siddique señaló que la familia de Ahmed lo contrató para acelerar su deportación porque temían que su salud se deteriorara en custodia.</p><p>Ahmed necesitaba un dispositivo para respirar, un spray nasal y medicamentos para sus condiciones crónicas, según Siddique, quien también mencionó hipertensión y una posible afección cardíaca.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-900000" name="module-900000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Antes del vuelo en julio, Ahmed había estado detenido en el centro de detención del Condado de Clay en Indiana, según Siddique.</p><p>Alrededor del 10 de junio, Siddique se puso en contacto con el centro de detención después de que la familia de Ahmed manifestara su preocupación sobre si estaba recibiendo los medicamentos recetados. Un oficial de la cárcel, contó Siddique, le aseguró que Ahmed los estaba recibiendo.</p><p>Siddique también habló directamente con Ahmed, quien le dijo que en ese momento estaba recibiendo la medicación pero que no podía confirmar si esto se hacía de forma constante. "Puede que la haya recibido cuando hablé con él, pero no sé si la recibía diariamente", dijo. "Eso no lo sé".</p><p>Dijo que notificó a ICE sobre las necesidades médicas de Ahmed y le informaron que esas preocupaciones serían remitidas al centro de detención.</p><p>Siddique afirmó que los funcionarios del Condado de Clay le dijeron repetidamente que los detenidos podían solicitar atención médica a través de tabletas electrónicas. Pero Ahmed no dominaba el inglés y Siddique cuestionó si podía usar correctamente el sistema.</p><p>El 18 de junio, Siddique supo que Ahmed había sido puesto en aislamiento médico. Dijo que un oficial del Condado de Clay citó claustrofobia, pero las circunstancias que rodearon el aislamiento no están claras. Describió el aislamiento médico como similar al confinamiento solitario, dejando a Ahmed solo en una celda.</p><p>Funcionarios del Condado de Clay confirmaron que Ahmed estuvo detenido allí pero no respondieron preguntas sobre su atención médica.</p><p>En los días previos a su deportación, Ahmed fue trasladado por varias instalaciones de detención, según Siddique. El 24 de julio Ahmed fue trasladado al Jackson Parrish Correctional Center en Luisiana; tres días después fue transferido a Camp East Montana en El Paso, Texas, y el 29 de julio al Prairieland Detention Center en Alvarado, Texas.</p><p>Siddique dijo que no sabe si Ahmed recibió su medicación recetada en cada centro o durante el vuelo de deportación. "Lo siguen transfiriendo, y entonces no estoy seguro si todo lo que necesitaba viajó con él", dijo Siddique.</p><p>Alexa Van Brunt, directora de la oficina de Illinois del MacArthur Justice Center, forma parte de un equipo legal que <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/11/09/demanda-por-derechos-civiles-denuncia-condiciones-inhumanas-en-centro-de-detencion-de-indiana" target="_blank" >recientemente presentó una demanda colectiva</a> que impugna las condiciones en Miami Correctional Facility, una prisión de Indiana que también aloja detenidos de ICE. La demanda alega atención médica inadecuada, retrasos en la entrega de medicamentos recetados, confinamiento solitario prolongado y condiciones insalubres.</p><p>Van Brunt dijo que las transferencias frecuentes entre instalaciones de detención representan otro riesgo para las personas con enfermedades crónicas. "Eso es otro impedimento para la atención adecuada porque no hay continuidad en la atención para personas con enfermedades crónicas como el cáncer o la diabetes", dijo.</p><p>Siddique dijo que siguió los traslados de Ahmed entre instalaciones a través de notificaciones de ICE, pero no recibió itinerario de vuelo ni actualizaciones durante el viaje.</p><p>Funcionarios de ICE dijeron que Ahmed fue autorizado médicamente para viajar y que ya no estaba bajo su custodia cuando murió. "No se produjeron emergencias médicas durante el vuelo, no se observaron señales de angustia médica y ninguna persona requirió hospitalización al aterrizar", dijo la agencia en un comunicado.</p><p>ICE afirmó que Ahmed recibió toda su medicación programada durante el vuelo. "Cualquier afirmación de negligencia o maltrato es categóricamente FALSA", dijo la agencia.</p><p>Pero después de que el avión aterrizó, Ahmed supuestamente se desplomó en la pista en Pakistán.</p><p>Siddique dijo que el hijo de Ahmed le envió un correo electrónico informándole que su padre murió siete horas después de aterrizar en Islamabad.</p><p>Funcionarios de ICE dijeron que una vez que Ahmed fue transferido a la custodia del gobierno pakistaní, ellos ya no tenían "autoridad sobre su atención ni acceso a sus registros médicos u oficiales".</p><p>La familia de Ahmed está evaluando acciones legales, según Siddique.</p><p>Algunos defensores de Chicago piden una investigación penal independiente sobre la muerte de Ahmed y los estándares médicos de ICE.</p><p>"Esta desgarradora y totalmente evitable tragedia pone al descubierto el desgarrador costo humano de una aplicación de la ley migratoria apresurada y agresiva", dijo Ahmed Rehab, director ejecutivo de CAIR-Chicago, en un comunicado.</p><p>El Consulado de Pakistán en Chicago y la Embajada de Pakistán no respondieron a las solicitudes de comentario.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Ferrara Candy Co. to close Little Village plant, lay off 154 workers
entries.summary: <p>Ferrara Candy Co. will shutter its Little Village manufacturing plant and lay off more than 150 employees in April.</p><p>The company announced plans to close its 31st Street facility in April 2027, citing “market conditions and our long-term innovation road map.”</p><p>Officials notified 154 employees and the state last week and said they plan to shift production to other facilities. The plant is at 2945 W. 31st St.</p><p>“Ferrara is deeply grateful to Chicago’s Little Village community for years of partnership and neighborly collaboration,” the company said in a statement.</p><p>Ferrara, whose brands include SweeTARTS, Brach’s and Nerds, began as a bakery in Little Italy in 1908 and has operated in Chicago for nearly 120 years. </p><p>The confectioner was acquired by Ferrero in 2017 but remains a privately held company under common ownership. Ferrara operates three other Chicago-area manufacturing facilities — in Bellwood, Forest Park and Itasca — and a fourth in DeKalb.</p><p>Ferrara said employees can continue working at the plant until it closes. Workers also have the opportunity to apply for open positions across Ferrara and its affiliate network.</p><p>The company said it will provide severance benefits and outplacement services to help affected employees find new jobs.</p><p>Employees were told of the planned closure last week, in compliance with the Worker Adjustment and Retraining Act, Ferrara said.</p><p>The Illinois Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification Act requires businesses with 75 or more employees to provide workers and the state with at least 60 days’ notice before plant closures or mass layoffs.</p><p>It’s not the first time Ferrara has closed a manufacturing plant.</p><p>In 2024, the company <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/money/2024/07/02/jelly-belly-ferrara-candy-closing-north-chicago-plant-laying-off-65-workers" target="_blank" >closed its Jelly Belly plant</a> in North Chicago, laying off 66 employees less than a year after acquiring family-owned Jelly Belly for an undisclosed amount.</p><p>That same year, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/money/2024/03/22/blommer-chocolate-close-chicago-factory" target="_blank" >Blommer Chocolate Co.</a> announced it would close its West Town factory, cutting 250 jobs, due to increasing costs of running the aging facility at 600 W. Kinzie St., cutting 250 jobs.</p>

entries.title: Grant Taylor's move to the White Sox rotation fits his boundary-pushing style
entries.summary: <p>LAS VEGAS — If Sean Burke’s emergence is paired with a healthy Davis Martin, <i>and</i> the White Sox land <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/11/10/white-sox-remain-set-on-adding-impact-starting-pitching-even-after-shifting-grant-taylor-to-rotation" target="_blank" ><u>the impact starters they’re seeking</u></a>, it’s at least possible to envision Grant Taylor joining a rotation that’s a strength next season.</p><p>It will still pale in comparison to the hype behind the LSU rotation he was set to head up with Paul Skenes, before Tommy John surgery ended Taylor’s collegiate career.</p><p>“If I had both of those suckers, that might have went down as one of the greatest pitching staffs of all time,” said University of Georgia head coach Wes Johnson, who ran the LSU pitching staff back in 2023. “You know who else was committed to come to LSU that we ended up losing was [Jacob] Misiorowski. The Brewers gave him his money.”</p><p>Before Johnson left his role as Twins pitching coach in 2022 to join LSU, he had already coached both of Taylor’s older brothers at Arkansas. Even without having pitched an actual game under Johnson, Taylor refers to him as “very pivotal in my life and my career,” and there remain traces of their work together in the way the right-hander’s wrist moves on his curveball, or how he coils on his back hip before exploding toward the plate.</p><p>But just as familiar to Johnson is the mindset Taylor exuded during his multiple marathon relief appearances in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox’</a> playoff run. It’s the same nature that will be present as Taylor adapts to starting in the majors, compiling innings loads he’s never approached before.</p><p>“One of the things I love about Grant is something you can say about a lot of good players,” Johnson told the Sun-Times. “The great ones can take their mind and push it to an uncomfortable place, and then challenge themselves there. Grant is one of the best at it that I’ve had in a while.”</p><p>Taylor’s game indicates as much. His fastball velocity is in the 96th percentile for MLB pitchers. His extension — the distance he stretches his body out from the pitching rubber to release the baseball — is 95th percentile, despite it being a category dominated by taller, lankier pitchers than the burly, 6-foot-3 Taylor.</p><p>After he suffered a lat strain in Low-A in 2024, and dealt with post-start soreness in Double-A in 2025, some in the organization wondered if Taylor pushed his body to the boundaries too much to hold up as a starter. In his assessments of Taylor as an amateur, Johnson said the right-hander drives more force into the ground with the front leg of his delivery than any pitcher he’s ever measured.</p><p>More than he’s struck out 32.5% of all big league hitters he’s faced, the White Sox are justifying Taylor’s move to the rotation with his clean health history in Chicago, and that he’s found a way to reliably harness his awesome power. Also, it’s not like staying healthy as a reliever is easier.</p><p>“There are some tremendous benefits with player health and production when going to the rotation, if they have certain attributes that will react well,” said general manager Chris Getz. “Based on what we've learned about Grant and what Grant has learned about himself in the major leagues, we felt it was the right time.”</p><p>“I’ve gotten really good at my routine,” Taylor said in mid-September. “It’s just being able to find that extra edge to take things up a notch every single day.”</p><p>Even as Taylor’s results waned in the Division Series against Cleveland, seemingly alongside extremely heavy usage, he largely held his velocity and insisted he physically felt up to the task at every turn.</p><p>Was that a testament to a 24-year-old whose consistency has grown in the last 18 months, and has fulfilled the terms for graduating to starting that the team laid out? Or is it a testament to a pitcher wired to push the limits of possibility until the day he has to be dragged off the field?</p><p>With Taylor, both are in play.</p><p>“There'll be a transition there,” Johnson said of Taylor starting. “But boy, I tell you what: man, that sucker's built different — mentally and physically.”</p>

entries.title: As Cubs chase pitching, how would they approach potentially replacing a third of their lineup?
entries.summary: <p>LAS VEGAS — The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> plan to focus most of their energy — and resources — this offseason on improving their pitching.</p><p>The goal, team president Jed Hoyer made clear, is to get the pitching staff closer in quality to the team’s position-player group, which led baseball in runs scored last season and had far and away the sport’s best defense.</p><p>But that position-player group isn’t getting carbon-copied over from 2026 to 2027.</p><p>A third of the lineup is on the free-agent market: left fielder Ian Happ, right fielder Seiya Suzuki and catcher Carson Kelly.</p><p>The Cubs <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/11/02/cubs-qualifying-offer-seiya-suzuki-free-agency-jed-hoyer-ian-happ-mlb-rumors" >extended Suzuki a qualifying offer</a>, a safeguard move that ensures they’ll receive a draft pick should he sign elsewhere. Given he’s one of the best free-agent hitters out there, he could very well be lured away as the Cubs focus on arms.</p><p>The Cubs aren’t closing the door on any of their free agents returning, though Hoyer said, “We’re not going to be able to bring back all of them.”</p><p>Happ has been a mainstay, an elite defender whose potential departure had tears flowing from teammates’ eyes the night the Cubs’ season ended.</p><p>Kelly, meanwhile, was excellent in two years as the team’s top catcher, swinging a bat that gave the Cubs an edge at a position that doesn’t always produce.</p><p>But should any or all find new gigs, the Cubs have plans for internal replacements.</p><p>In the corner-outfield spots that were this year manned by two Gold Glove finalists, the Cubs plan to turn to infielders in Matt Shaw and Pedro Ramirez.</p><p>Shaw played plenty of outfield in 2026 after Alex Bregman’s arrival moved him from third base. Though he was limited by injuries, Shaw received praise for his work.</p><p>Ramirez doesn’t have even that minimal experience. But the Cubs spent the 2026 season lauding him as a wise-beyond-his-years rookie, and there’s confidence he could handle a position change, too.</p><p>“Pedro’s someone I could see playing in the outfield for us and will need to put himself in a better position defensively to do that,” general manager Carter Hawkins said Tuesday during the GM meetings. “But I have a lot of confidence he’ll be able to make those adjustments and be even more versatile than he already is.</p><p>“When you have someone that’s athletic, that’s willing to work, willing to listen, they can do a lot of things you didn’t think they could do.”</p><p>Behind the plate, the top job would go to Miguel Amaya, whose Cubs tenure predates Kelly’s. He played 117 games in 2024 before shining with the bat in 2025, when he posted a 127 OPS-plus.</p><p>Those numbers dipped last season, his OPS-plus down to a below-average 98, but the Cubs were impressed with how he performed in the many other facets of a big league catching job.</p><p>“We’ve all seen a little more out of Miggy offensively,” Hawkins said, “and that’s the expectation, that he gets himself in shape physically and mentally to have a type of offensive year that we know he can have in 2027.”</p><p>The Cubs are also high on minor league backstop Owen Ayers, their No. 2 ranked prospect who played at three different levels last season, with a .929 OPS, 25 home runs and 82 walks in 125 games.</p><p>“We’re going to figure out where we’re going to allocate our resources over the course of the next few weeks,” Hawkins said. “That could be at the catcher position. It could be that we stick internally. But it’s an area where people are going to need to step up.</p><p>“Carson was a great player for us the last couple of years. It could be Carson that steps up for us. But someone’s going to need to step up and fill those wins, and we’re excited about our ability to do that.”</p>

entries.title: Taking care of business; Chicago's first self-cleaning public restroom opens in Polish Triangle
entries.summary: <p>Christian Malatesta wanted to go first.</p><p>When he heard the 1st Ward, where he lives, was getting Chicago's first self-cleaning public restroom, Malatesta emailed local Ald. Daniel La Spata to ask for the first spot in line.</p><p>Malatesta, 35, had used a similar facility in Paris, and was excited to see the technology come to Chicago.</p><p>“I don't think you should have to buy a $5 cup of coffee to use the restroom,” he said.</p><p>His big moment arrived Wednesday, when La Spata and JCDecaux, the company providing and operating the facility, officially opened it to the public.</p><p>Located near the CTA's Division Street Blue Line station, the facility is designed for one user at a time. Visitors press a button to open the sliding door. Inside, there's a bright blue wall and a map of Chicago and plenty of space to move about comfortably. When they've left, an integrated system washes and disinfects the toilet and floor after each use.</p><p>The experience, Malatesta said, was straightforward.</p><p>“Everything was labeled very clearly, and everything was where I expected it to be,” Malatesta said. “You just press the button, the door opens for you, it flushes for you.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-280000" name="image-280000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4ba04b4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F15%2Fe4%2Faa37d56d4975b51b827a77d3ad52%2Fwesttowntoilet-261112-18.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0618aea/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F15%2Fe4%2Faa37d56d4975b51b827a77d3ad52%2Fwesttowntoilet-261112-18.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4582bd6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F15%2Fe4%2Faa37d56d4975b51b827a77d3ad52%2Fwesttowntoilet-261112-18.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Ald. Daniel La Spata (1st) speaks while holding his daughter during a press conference Wednesday celebrating the opening of Chicago’s first automated self-clearning public toilet.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The facility will operate from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. as part of the city's Coordinated Street Furniture Program, managed by the Chicago Department of Transportation in coordination with the Office of the Chief Financial Officer and delivered by JCDecaux.</p><p>The restroom is free to use, and JCDecaux is providing and maintaining the facility at no cost to the city. Installation, however, cost <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/10/03/chicago-self-cleaning-toilet-what-to-know?utm_source=chatgpt.com" target="_blank" >more than $400,000, including plumbing</a>. La Spata's office said those costs were covered by the so-called "menu money" allocated to each alderperson to spend on infrastructure projects in their ward at their discretion.</p><p>The city will evaluate the pilot based on safety and use, La Spata said. He suggested assessing it after about a year and said the city expects to receive monthly usage statistics from JCDecaux.</p><p>“I really believe in a future in Chicago, where we really live into our identity as a global city,” La Spata said. “Global cities provide this amenity to all of their residents.”</p><p>This amenity will serve more than just commuters heading to and from the L. It's in a busy area, where Milwaukee and Ashland avenues and Division Street come together in West Town, near Wicker Park and Ukrainian Village.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div entries.title: Kyle Davidson addresses Blackhawks' disastrous start: Mark Eaton changing roles, trades being explored
entries.summary: <p>It turns out <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/11/10/blackhawks-goalies-spencer-knight-arvid-soderblom-drew-commesso" >switching</a> backup goalies is not the only change the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> are making after their disastrous 4-13-1 start.</p><p>It's one of two changes, in fact.</p><p>The other is bringing in former NHL defenseman Mark Eaton, who has been the Hawks' assistant general manager overseeing prospect development for the past five years, to join the coaching staff and work directly with the team's struggling young NHL defensemen.</p><p>It's a decent idea, to be fair. But for that to be the only change revealed throughout GM Kyle Davidson's 45-minute news conference Wednesday is surely and justifiably disappointing to fans.</p><p>"This is akin to something you see in the NFL with a position coach," Davidson said. "[He will be] hyper-focused on improving individual defending skills, in this case, and not necessarily impacting the overall scheme.</p><p>"A lot of what [Eaton] built his career on are things that our players need to get better at. So he's uniquely qualified from that perspective, as well as the fact he's worked with almost every one of our defensemen since they’ve been drafted. He knows how they learn, he knows their gaps, he knows how they communicate and he's also got that personal relationship with them."</p><p>Davidson also said he's actively seeking out trades, which — if they come to fruition — would obviously extend the list of changes. None have yet, though.</p><p>It seems that's mostly because other, less desperate teams are reluctant to make moves this early in the season unless blown away by an offer.</p><p>"This is a little bit of a precarious time where you don't want to do something for the sake of doing something and make a mistake that you're going to regret later," he said. "So that's something top of mind. But that doesn't change our intent."</p><p>Davidson made it clear experience is the No. 1 trait they're prioritizing in trade targets, and defensive reliability is No. 2. He believes they need more players who are comfortable in the NHL and can be calming influences in chaotic situations.</p><p>But it would be insane to use assets to acquire a rental — in other words, a pending 2027 free agent — given how far out of the playoff race the Hawks already are this season. So they need a player with contract term, and those are even scarcer in this market.</p><p>It likely would've been easier to acquire another defense-oriented veteran or two during the offseason, and Davidson conceded he erred by not doing so. </p><p>"We probably, I don't want to say 'took for granted,' but perhaps miscalculated a little bit on [how] we would look if we had one of our relied-upon defensemen go down," he said, alluding to Bowen Byram <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/11/02/blackhawks-bowen-byram-injury-timeline-specialist" >missing</a> 12 of 18 games so far.</p><p>"Could we have benefited from one more veteran? It's very possible we may have. That's part of the evaluation process and honest candor that we're having internally."</p><p>Byram did finally rejoin the Hawks for practice Wednesday, as did injured star forward Patrick Kane, although both wore non-contact jerseys and declined to speak to reporters afterward.</p><p>Davidson insisted Byram's upper-body injury, which has lingered for a month now, isn't considered a long-term concern. However, he was frank when evaluating the Hawks' on-ice struggles and — in particular — their defensive ineptitude.</p><p>"Simply put, we've not been good enough," Davidson said. "This isn't what we told our fans to expect. I take responsibility in this.</p><p>"We're not defending well enough. We give up odd-man rushes — specifically two-on-ones and breakaways — at a rate that's one of the highest in the league. As well as the high-danger chances that we're giving up at too high of a rate in our defensive zone, which obviously then leads to goals against."</p><h3><b>More of the same</b></h3><p>Aside from those aforementioned subjects, most of Davidson's messaging Wednesday sounded eerily similar to what he has been saying for years.</p><p>Much of it isn't incorrect by any means — for example, the development of young players does indeed require time and patience — but it has nonetheless grown old to fans who have maintained patience for a while already.</p><p>"I can confidently say that we...have acquired through the draft — and other means — some very meaningful foundational pieces that are going to be great-to-elite players in this league," Davidson said. "[They] will carry this team upwards as these younger players reach their prime."</p><p>"We're seeing maybe some of the downside, at times, of having such a young center and young defensive corps," he said later. "But they’re gaining this experience that is going to serve them well."</p><p>Davidson reasserted his support for oft-criticized coach Jeff Blashill, too.</p><p>"The players believe in him. He's made them better," he said. "I've seen this perception out there that he's stubborn and he doesn't want to change. I contradict that based on my experience with 'Blash.' In our conversations, he's someone that seeks out feedback, wants alternative opinions.</p><p>"We’re very much on the same page with how we assess the team and how we think we can be better moving forward."</p><p>Davidson said Hawks chairman Danny Wirtz, who hasn't spoken to reporters since giving Davidson a contract extension in April, is "disappointed like all of us" by the start. Davidson said he and Wirtz "talk almost daily," having "productive but honest" conversations.</p><p>Asked if he's considered bringing any new voices into the front office — in the same vein as bringing Eaton into the coaching staff — Davidson mentioned hiring contract-negotiation specialist Chris O'Hearn in January 2025.</p><p>"There’s value in having strong opinions and opinions that will challenge yourself, which we certainly do," Davidson said. "This is not a 'yes man' scenario that we have within our group. </p><p>"If I wasn't getting the proper feedback or different opinions, or there wasn’t good constructive discussion in the room, then I would probably agree that some other look is good. But I don't feel like we've stagnated."</p>

entries.title: ‘Heartbreaking and entirely preventable’: Chicago-area man died after deportation, family says
entries.summary: <p>A Chicago area-man, who had no criminal record and suffered from multiple chronic health conditions, died shortly after a deportation flight to Pakistan, his family says.</p><p>Sixty-one-year-old Ayaz Ahmed of Morton Grove was arrested in June by Immigration and Customs Enforcement and faced deportation for having an expired visa, said his attorney Hashim Siddique.</p><p>Ahmed’s daughter said the family tried to expedite his deportation because they feared his health would deteriorate in custody.</p><p>“The fight was not about letting my dad go, the fight was literally about just getting him the medical attention he needed,” Saleah Sahar said.</p><p>Sahar described her father as “the heart of the family,” a hardworking man who was close to his children. She said he worked long hours, paid his bills and called his children constantly while in detention, sometimes just to hear their voices.</p><p>“Even if he had nothing to say, he would call,” she said.</p><p>Ahmed had diabetes, high blood pressure and sleep apnea. He required daily insulin, metformin, a breathing device, and nasal spray, according to his daughter. She said he had a stent placed in a coronary artery in December 2025 and had also undergone knee replacement surgery. She added that she helped him with his evening medications when they lived together.</p><p>Prior to the July flight to Pakistan, Ahmed had been detained at the Clay County Detention center in Indiana, according to Siddique.</p><p>Around June 10, Siddique contacted the detention center after Ahmed’s family raised concerns about whether he was receiving prescribed medication. A jail officer, Siddique shared, assured him that Ahmed was receiving them.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided by family</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>But Ahmed’s daughter said her father repeatedly complained that he was not getting his medication. She said she mailed the medication to the detention center and emailed officials the tracking number, but Ahmed later told her a nurse said she did not have it.</p><p>Sahar said her father told her he spent two days in medical isolation after experiencing breathing difficulties. He was so frightened by the experience, she said, that he promised a nurse he would stop asking for medication if she returned him to the general detention population.</p><p>“I told them I will never bother them for my medication again,” Sahar recalled him saying. Sahar said an ICE officer told her Ahmed “must have misbehaved” when she called to ask why he had been placed in isolation.</p><p>Siddique also spoke directly with Ahmed who told him he was getting the medication at that time but he could not confirm whether this was being done consistently.</p><p>“He may have been [receiving his medication] when I spoke to him, but I don’t know if he was receiving it daily,” he said.</p><p>Siddique said he notified ICE of Ahmed’s medical needs and was told those concerns would be forwarded to the detention center.</p><p>Siddque said Clay County officials repeatedly told him that detainees could request medical care through electronic tablets. But Ahmed was not fluent in English and Siddique questioned whether he was able to properly use the system.</p><p>Clay County officials confirmed Ahmed was in detention there but would not answer questions about his medical care.</p><p>In the days before his deportation, Ahmed was transferred through several detention facilities, according to Siddique. On July 24 Ahmed was moved to Jackson Parrish Correctional Center in Louisiana, three days later he was transferred to Camp East Montana in El Paso, Texas, and on July 29 to Prairieland Detention Center in Alvarado, Texas.</p><p>Siddique said he does not know whether Ahmed received his prescribed medication at each facility or during the deportation flight.</p><p>“He keeps getting transferred, and then I’m not sure if everything went with him,” Siddique said.</p><p>Alexa Van Brunt, director of the Illinois office of the MacArthur Justice Center, is part of a legal team that recently filed a class-action lawsuit challenging conditions at Miami Correctional Facility, an Indiana prison that also holds ICE detainees. The lawsuit alleges inadequate medical care, delays in receiving prescribed medications, prolonged solitary confinement and unsanitary conditions.</p><p>Van Brunt said frequent transfers between detention facilities pose another risk for people with chronic illnesses.</p><p>“That’s another impediment to proper care because there’s no continuity of care for people with chronic diseases like cancer or diabetes,” she said.</p><p>Siddique said he tracked Ahmed’s transfers between detention facilities through ICE notifications but received no flight itinerary or updates during the journey. ICE officials said Ahmed was medically cleared for travel and was no longer in their custody when he died.</p><p>“No medical emergencies occurred during the flight, no signs of medical distress were observed, and no individuals required hospitalization upon landing,” the agency said in a statement.</p><p>ICE said Ahmed boarded a flight to Pakistan on July 23 and received all of his scheduled medication during the flight.</p><p>“Any claims of neglect or mistreatment are categorically FALSE,” the agency said in a statement.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div They told her his health deteriorated during the journey.</p><p>After the plane landed, Ahmed allegedly collapsed on the tarmac in Pakistan.</p><p>Sahar said the family still does not know exactly when or how Ahmed died. She said they learned of his death on Aug. 3, after spending three days trying to locate him in Pakistan. When his usual phone calls stopped, the family contacted Pakistani officials and asked relatives to help find him. A cousin eventually traveled to Islamabad, where the family learned he had died.</p><p>Sahar said she and her family were unable to attend his burial in Pakistan.</p><p>ICE officials said that once Ahmed was transferred to the custody of the Pakistani government, they no longer had “authority over their care or access to their medical or official records.”</p><p>Ahmed’s family is exploring legal action and is still seeking a civil rights attorney, according to Siddique and Ahmed’s daughter, Saleha Sahar.</p><p>Some Chicago advocates are calling for an independent criminal investigation into Ahmed’s death and ICE’s medical standards.</p><p>“This heartbreaking and entirely preventable tragedy lays bare the harrowing human cost of rushed, aggressive immigration enforcement,” Ahmed Rehab, executive director of CAIR-Chicago, said in a statement.</p><p>The Pakistan Consulate in Chicago and the Pakistani Embassy did not respond to requests for comment.</p>

entries.title: Sexual assault suspect pawned two PlayStations stolen from victim in Auburn Gresham attack, prosecutors say
entries.summary: <p>A 53-year-old man who sexually assaulted his neighbor at gunpoint fled with several items including two PlayStation systems, prosecutors said Wednesday during his first hearing after being charged in the attack. </p><p>During the hearing, a Cook County judge ordered Calvin Lindsey detained and prosecutors laid out details of the Friday morning assault in the 7700 block of South Racine Avenue.</p><p>The attack began shortly after the 19-year-old woman had returned to her apartment after taking her dogs to the backyard. She locked the back door , then went to her bedroom and closed that door, prosecutors said in court. </p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/11/10/cops-question-person-of-interest-after-home-invasion-sexual-assault-at-gunpoint-in-auburn-gresham" target="_blank" >About 10:35 a.m., Lindsey burst into her home</a> through the back door. He was wearing a navy blue jacket with its hood up, black pants, red and white gym shoes, a baseball cap with a red bill and a face mask that looked like a medical or painters mask, prosecutors said.</p><p>He barged into her bedroom and asked for money before forcing her to go into a bathroom, where he sexually assaulted her, prosecutors said. </p><p>Lindsey then ransacked the apartment before fleeing about 11:07 a.m. with several items, including the two gaming systems, prosecutors said.</p><p>Lindsey was spotted on doorbell camera footage leaving with a backpack and a white garbage bag, prosecutors said. He was later found to have taken the two video game systems as well as the woman's cell phone and purse and another person's gun, prosecutors said. </p><p>About noon, an individual wearing the same "distinctive" shoes and hat was captured on a bank camera video getting out of a black SUV, removing a white bag and backpack from the cargo area of the car before entering Ashland Pawners and Jewelers, 1543 W. 47th St., prosecutors said. </p><p>The shop provided records of Lindsey pawning two gaming systems, and he was identified in a photo array, prosecutors said. </p><p>After the attack, the 19-year-old, who does not know Lindsey, immediately cried out to her mother and to a roommate. </p><p>The victim was taken to a hospital by paramedics. The woman <a class="Link" href="https://abc7chicago.com/post/auburn-gresham-chicago-crime-person-interest-custody-home-invasion-sex-assault/20030262/" target="_blank" >told ABC7 that she waited more than four hours</a> for police to arrive after calling 911 multiple times.</p><p>Prosecutors also secured an order of protection, which said Lindsey was prohibited from "knowingly coming or remaining within 2,500 feet away" from the woman at her home or place of work, court documents show. </p><p>Lindsey, of the Auburn Gresham neighborhood, is due back in court Monday. </p>

entries.title: Signing Day: Jamier Montgomery's rise from sitting out freshman year to a Kent State scholarship
entries.summary: <p>Freshman year, Jamier Montgomery was an ineligible player on a Public League White Division basketball team. He spent this summer playing for an independent club basketball team outside of the two major circuits. It is not an easy road from there to a Division I basketball scholarship, especially in today's college basketball landscape.</p><p>But Wednesday at Crane, Montgomery and his family officially pulled off the feat when he signed with Kent State.</p><p>Montgomery started high school at Warren, so he couldn’t play his first year after transferring to Crane a few months later. His mother and grandfather are Crane graduates, and his dad, Archie Boyd, played at Farragut and Crane.</p><p>“I am proud beyond words,” Boyd said. “I can’t explain how proud I feel that he is in this situation where he will be able to succeed. He’s a good kid that gets good grades. And now he can go to school for free.”</p><p>Sitting out freshman year was difficult for Montgomery.</p><p>“He went through a depression a little bit,” Lanae Montgomery, Jamier’s mom, said. “It was a bad year for him. But that pushed him a lot more. He kept telling me he had a chip on his shoulder.”</p><p>“That gave him the urgency to do better,” Boyd said. “He felt counted out. I was able to understand that. I was counted out in high school, and when you come out with that chip on your shoulder, it is different.”</p><p>Sophomore year, Montgomery immediately showed his smooth overall game and his potential was clear. There were kinks to work out, and that started to happen this summer.</p><p>“He blew up,” Crane coach Mekiel Posey said. “It happened pretty fast with the college attention. But I always knew it was coming. He’s a gym rat, a guy you have to kick out. I knew we would be at this moment because of the work he puts in.”</p><p>Montgomery played football and baseball before basketball. When he came to his dad and asked about basketball, everything changed.</p><p>“I said if we start that, there is no turning back. You have to be serious about the game,” Boyd said. “But he wanted it. He woke me up at six in the morning the next day; we went to the court and never looked back.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-c60000" name="image-c60000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e8937bd/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5803x3257+0+307/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F58%2F76%2F4f83ef4a41fe8a394e14f13ca322%2Fob-cst-111226-005.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4c18f4a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5803x3257+0+307/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F58%2F76%2F4f83ef4a41fe8a394e14f13ca322%2Fob-cst-111226-005.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f2b329a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5803x3257+0+307/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F58%2F76%2F4f83ef4a41fe8a394e14f13ca322%2Fob-cst-111226-005.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Crane’s Jamier Montgomery poses for a photo with teammates on Signing Day. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f2b329a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5803x3257+0+307/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F58%2F76%2F4f83ef4a41fe8a394e14f13ca322%2Fob-cst-111226-005.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b8c0652/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5803x3257+0+307/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F58%2F76%2F4f83ef4a41fe8a394e14f13ca322%2Fob-cst-111226-005.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f2b329a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5803x3257+0+307/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F58%2F76%2F4f83ef4a41fe8a394e14f13ca322%2Fob-cst-111226-005.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Crane’s Jamier Montgomery poses for a photo with teammates on Signing Day.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Kirsten Stickney/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Montgomery, a 6-2 guard, also had offers from Western Illinois and Akron.</p><p>“Starting off learning with my dad was chill, but then it got intense,” Montgomery said. “Any time and any place we could play basketball, we took advantage of it.</p><p>“Then I had to focus on improving my grades after freshman year. I had to improve in the classroom before the court.”</p><p>Montgomery’s rise would have stood out a decade ago when a few dozen local players typically signed with Division I colleges. It’s much more notable this year, when just six local players on the area’s 400 high schools are signing Division I scholarships.</p><p>“Our visit to Kent State was amazing,” Lanae Montgomery said. “The experience was great, and I think we all felt it right away. But I made sure to keep quiet and stay in the background and let him make his decision.”</p><p>Montgomery averaged 11 points as a sophomore and 14 points, 3.4 rebounds, and 2 steals as a junior. He’ll be Crane's focal point and leader this season and a marked man in every game as the Public League's best player.</p><p>“I’m looking forward to making it downstate,” Montgomery said. “That’s my main goal for sure.”</p><h3>2026 Signing Day</h3><p>The complete list of seniors that have committed to Division I schools as of Nov. 12, 2026. Please send additions and corrections to <a class="Link" href="mailto:mobrien@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >mobrien@suntimes.com</a>.</p><p>Mason Martin, Neuqua Valley, <b>Illinois</b></p><p>Jamier Montgomery, Crane,<b> Kent State</b></p><p>Markese Peoples, St. Laurence,<b> UIC</b></p><p>Hayden Schroeder, Wheaton Academy, <b>Pennsylvania</b></p><p>Alex Sirbu, Buffalo Grove,<b> Columbia</b></p><p>Edward Stasys, Benet, <b>Yale</b></p>

entries.title: Will the Illinois House elect its first woman speaker? Dems float potential contenders to replace Welch
entries.summary: <p>After this week’s bombshell announcement that Illinois’ first Black House speaker <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/11/05/illinois-house-speaker-chris-welch-mutiny-26-democrats-call-for-new-leader-harry-benton-scandal" target="_blank" ><u>wouldn’t seek a fourth term</u></a>, Democratic state legislators could blaze another new trail with their selection for the next leader of their chamber.</p><p>Five women lawmakers were among the names floated most frequently as the Sun-Times spoke on background with more than a dozen lawmakers, lobbyists and other insiders sizing up potential candidates to replace outgoing House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch, D-Hillside.</p><p>Many said it was time for Illinois to see its first woman speaker to help uproot an entrenched culture of sexual harassment following the Capitol’s latest scandal.</p><p>Welch lost the support of most of his caucus in the wake of his <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/08/05/welch-benton-harassment-working-group-cassidy" target="_blank" ><u>delayed response</u></a> to misconduct allegations against disgraced ex-state Rep. Harry Benton, D-Plainfield — just like Welch’s longtime predecessor, imprisoned ex-Speaker Michael Madigan, was felled amid criticism of his inaction on complaints within his political organization.</p><p>There has scarcely been a question about the occupancy of the speaker’s office since Madigan first tightened his iron grip on the gavel in 1983. And even for a brief interlude of Republican House control in 1995-96, Lee Daniels was a clear pick to shift from GOP minority leader.</p><p>Now, for the first time in four decades, legislators have adequate time to seriously consider a field of representatives to step up in their chamber, without an incumbent or another obvious power player towering over the election for speaker.</p><p>Welch was a late entry in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2021/1/13/22228758/emanuel-chris-welch-illinois-house-speaker-vote-mike-madigan" target="_blank" ><u>the 2021 intra-party race</u></a> after Madigan’s stunning announcement he was stepping down, prompting <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2021/1/12/22227890/sources-latinx-caucus-latino-welch-hispanic-house-speaker-black-madigan-hernandez-williams-kifowit" target="_blank" ><u>a chaotic scramble for votes</u></a> over the final day of a lame-duck legislative session — a power grab that didn’t even play out in the Capitol itself. Lawmakers were masked and socially distanced in a Springfield convention center in the depths of the COVID-19 pandemic.</p><p>“By the time [Madigan] suspended his campaign, there were 24 hours for us to make a decision,” said North Side state Rep. Kelly Cassidy, one of the legislators who led the movement for new leadership. “That’s not a healthy way for us to do this.</p><p>“We have an actual chance to put thought into this that we didn’t get to before, and to hear from our colleagues about their visions. We have such an array of experience and talent throughout every corner of our caucus,” Cassidy said — noting she’s “not even remotely” interested in the post herself.</p><p>Asked if it’s time for a female speaker, Gov. JB Pritzker said “that's going to be up to the members.”</p><p>“What I know is that anybody who has been sexually harassed or had anything like that happen to them should know what the process is for reporting that,” Pritzker said at an unrelated news conference Friday. “The House is really responsible for getting their house in order… Every company, every nonprofit, virtually everybody I know, has developed a process for their institutions to deal with these things. It should be no different for the House of Representatives.”</p><p>Maneuvering behind closed doors will accelerate during the fall veto session that starts Nov. 17, reaching a political crescendo with the speaker's election in January immediately after the 105th General Assembly is sworn in.</p><p>The Sun-Times identified just one hat officially thrown into the ring by Friday morning, but plenty more will be in the weeks ahead. Here are eight names to watch, with more guaranteed to follow in the race for 60 votes:</p><h3>State Rep. Eva-Dina Delgado, D-Chicago</h3><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-a70000" name="image-a70000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9a61f73/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+369/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F19%2Fc5%2Ff41de11f4fbebe22a20eb969d61a%2Ftransit-102424-6.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8efefc0/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+369/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F19%2Fc5%2Ff41de11f4fbebe22a20eb969d61a%2Ftransit-102424-6.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/263c9a6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+369/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F19%2Fc5%2Ff41de11f4fbebe22a20eb969d61a%2Ftransit-102424-6.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="State Rep. Eva-Dina Delgado, D-Chicago, speaks during a Chicago news conference in 2024.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Delgado's name stood out on the list of 26 lawmakers who signed a letter Thursday calling for a new speaker, the statement that spelled doom for Welch's tenure. An assistant majority leader for Welch, the Northwest Side representative who just locked up a fifth term has been a key shepherd of state budgets — the chamber's most unwieldy annual legislative lift — and last year she spearheaded landmark transit reform legislation along with another potential speaker contender. </p><h3>State Rep. Jehan Gordon-Booth, D-Peoria</h3><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-5c0000" name="image-5c0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/33579db/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+369/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd1%2Fad%2Ff9e1b0e04f539e00ca1c002b82c2%2Fpritzkerbudget-060624-3.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2a91c4b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+369/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd1%2Fad%2Ff9e1b0e04f539e00ca1c002b82c2%2Fpritzkerbudget-060624-3.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6f0e121/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+369/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd1%2Fad%2Ff9e1b0e04f539e00ca1c002b82c2%2Fpritzkerbudget-060624-3.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch, D-Hillside, stands beside state Rep. Mary Beth Canty, D-Arlington Heights, speaks at a Loop news conference in 2024.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Canty, who joined Cassidy in publicly calling for Welch to step aside, chairs the House Democratic Women’s Caucus as she enters a third term representing a district at the center of the Chicago Bears stadium debate. </p><p>She took herself out of consideration Nov. 10, saying she was "humbled by the outreach."</p><p>"I want a speaker who is prepared to strengthen House Democrats as a whole, both legislatively and politically, with a leadership team that reflects our caucus and a staff that is empowered an engaged," Canty said in a statement. </p>
